breaks.summary: Votes stop being transactions on chain: validators send them directly to each other. Initially a validator admission ticket reproduces the incentives of today's vote transaction fees. Voting is not invisible afterwards: for rewards, the leader of slot s+8 can post up to two vote aggregates for slot s. Code that reads individual vote transactions out of blocks no longer finds them.
Optimistic confirmation is superseded by faster actual finality; the SIMD names this as the most visible change.

fix.summary: Do not derive validator activity from vote transactions in blocks, and review code that relies on optimistic confirmation as something distinct from finality.

sources.note: Document status at retrieval is Review; the front matter feature field is still a placeholder, the gate address comes from agave. Backwards compatibility is stated as Incompatible: Alpenglow replaces the old consensus protocol with all its voting logic.

breaks.summary: EIP-7702 breaks the invariant that msg.sender == tx.origin holds only in the top frame of a transaction: a delegated account can make several calls in one transaction. Reentrancy guards of the style require(tx.origin == msg.sender) and atomic sandwich protections that rely on tx.origin no longer hold. Using that check only to know that the sender is an EOA is, by the EIP's own reading, not affected.

An account delegated under EIP-7702 has code: the delegation indicator, 0xef0100 followed by the address of the delegate, and EXTCODESIZE returns 23 for it. A check that reads code as "a contract" or no code as "an EOA" — an isContract call, a test of code.length or extcodesize — now takes a delegated EOA for a contract.

OpenZeppelin's SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow checks an ECDSA signature only when the signer has no code, and otherwise asks the signer for ERC-1271. A delegated EOA has code, so its ECDSA signature is not checked as such: it is valid only if the delegate implements ERC-1271 and accepts it.

OpenZeppelin's ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received calls onERC721Received on any recipient with code, and reverts when the call fails or returns another value. A safe transfer or a safe mint to a delegated EOA reverts unless its delegate implements the receiver.
eth_getCode of a delegated EOA returns the 23-byte delegation indicator, and the account still sends transactions. Telling contracts from EOAs by whether eth_getCode is empty no longer works.

detect.summary: Compares msg.sender with tx.origin. As a reentrancy guard or a sandwich protection it no longer holds after EIP-7702; as a test that the sender is an EOA it does — a person has to tell which.

Calls isContract, which tells contracts from EOAs by their code; a delegated EOA has code. Most calls only check that an address set by an administrator is deployed, which EIP-7702 does not change: look at the ones that decide how to treat a caller, a recipient or a signer.
Treats an account without code as an EOA (code.length == 0): a delegated EOA has code and takes the other branch — for a signature that is ERC-1271, for a recipient a receiver hook.

probe.expect: The transaction has type 0x4 and an authorization list of one authorization.

detect.summary: An Ethereum provider returns a set-code transaction (type 4) with its authorization list. A provider that drops the list, or fails on the type, hides delegations from whatever reads through it.

probe.expect: The transaction has type 0x4 and an authorization list of one authorization.

fix.summary: Replace a reentrancy guard built on tx.origin == msg.sender with one held in a transient storage variable, as the EIP suggests. A sandwich protection built on tx.origin has no replacement in the EIP, which calls relying on it a bad practice: it has to be designed again, not patched.

Where it matters whether an account is a delegated EOA, read the first three bytes of its code: 0xef0100 marks the delegation indicator (OpenZeppelin's EIP7702Utils.fetchDelegate returns the delegate), and decide explicitly how such an account is treated — for a signature, ECDSA, ERC-1271, or both.
A contract meant to be a delegate implements the receiver hooks the accounts that delegate to it rely on, such as onERC721Received: OpenZeppelin's ERC721Utils calls it on every recipient with code.

breaks.summary: The minimum balance of an account is (128 + data size in bytes) * lamports_per_byte, and every step lowers lamports_per_byte. An account funded at an earlier, higher minimum keeps the difference: the SIMD allows reducing the balance to the new minimum, it does not return anything by itself.

A lamports_per_byte value compiled into a client or program goes stale at every step: on activation the value changes in the bank and in the Rent sysvar, while DEFAULT_LAMPORTS_PER_BYTE in the SDKs is updated only after activation. The SIMD calls the reduction strictly a relaxation: existing program logic keeps working, so a stale higher constant overpays rather than fails.

The reduction is not guaranteed to be one-way. The SIMD states that rent can be increased back to the legacy value in case of excessive state growth, noting that SIMD-0392 allows this without significant disruption to existing accounts; agave already declares a gate set_lamports_per_byte_to_6960, registered as "SIMD-0438: Reset lamports per byte to legacy value of 6960". A minimum balance fixed at a reduced value can therefore become too low for newly created accounts.

fix.summary: Take the minimum balance from the cluster at run time (the Rent sysvar in programs, getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption in clients) instead of a compiled-in lamports_per_byte.

sources.note: Document status at retrieval is Idea; the front matter feature field is still a placeholder. The SIMD makes each later step conditional on a risk analysis, so the five steps are a schedule, not a commitment.

Five modules set_lamports_per_byte_to_6333 through _696, registered as "SIMD-0437-1" to "SIMD-0437-5", each with its LAMPORTS_PER_BYTE constant. A sixth module, set_lamports_per_byte_to_6960, belongs to SIMD-0438 and is not a gate of this entry.
The sysvar holds 5080; getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption(0) returns 650240, which is 128 * 5080. devnet returned the same values at slot 500339413.

breaks.summary: A duration expressed in slots shrinks in wall-clock time with every stage: the SIMD tells dapp developers and off-chain services to stop assuming that 400 ms * slots is a stable conversion. A timer of N slots lasts half as long at 200 ms as it did at 400 ms.

SDK constants stay at their 400 ms values at first: static constants for default slot duration, ticks per second, slots per year and slot-to-time conversion may keep describing 400 ms while the cluster runs 350, 300, 250 or 200 ms banks.

Per-slot limits scale down in proportion to the slot time so that the wall-clock rate stays approximately the same. From the 400 ms baseline of 60,000,000 the maximum block compute units become 37,500,000 at 250 ms and 30,000,000 at 200 ms; the maximum writable-account compute units go from 24,000,000 to 15,000,000 and 12,000,000. The ratios apply to whatever baseline is active: with the 100,000,000 block limit of SIMD-0286 the values are 62,500,000 and 50,000,000. Code tuned to the per-block or per-account limit of a 400 ms slot exceeds the scaled one.
An epoch stays 432,000 slots, so it lasts half as long at 200 ms as at 400 ms. Anything scheduled per epoch happens twice as often in wall-clock time.

fix.summary: Keep slot counts only where slot semantics are intended; where a duration means wall-clock time, do not derive it from a fixed milliseconds-per-slot constant. The SIMD advises preferring cluster-provided timing parameters once they are available.

breaks.summary: getTransaction, and getBlock with transactionDetails full or accounts, fail with JSON-RPC error -32015 "Transaction version (1) is not supported by the requesting client" when the request omits maxSupportedTransactionVersion or sets it to 0 and the result contains a version 1 transaction. getBlock with transactionDetails signatures or none is not affected.
A serialized version 1 transaction starts with the version byte 129 (0x81). A decoder written for the legacy and version 0 layouts has no branch for that value.

@solana/kit 8.0.0 removed three compute-unit-limit helpers from @solana/kit in favour of resource-limit helpers that also set the loaded accounts data size limit for version 1 transactions, and removed the fixed transaction size constants from @solana/transactions because version 1 transactions have a larger size limit.
The maximum size of a version 1 transaction is 4096 bytes; the prior maximum was 1232. A buffer or a size check fixed at 1232 bytes is too small for a valid version 1 transaction.

@solana/web3.js 1.98.4 cannot read a version 1 transaction even when maxSupportedTransactionVersion is 1: getTransaction and getParsedTransaction throw a StructError on the version field, and getBlock fails the same way. 1.99.0 reads all three and returns a MessageV1.

detect.summary: RPC read call pins maxSupportedTransactionVersion to the literal 0; it fails as soon as the result contains a version 1 transaction.
The Rust RPC client config pins max_supported_transaction_version to Some(0); reads fail as soon as the result contains a version 1 transaction.
The Go RPC client names version 0 through the SDK constant or a uint64(0) value; reads fail as soon as the result contains a version 1 transaction.

A transaction or block is read without maxSupportedTransactionVersion, which the RPC treats like the lowest version. Check that this is a Solana RPC call: libraries of other chains use the same method names.
The Python RPC client is called with max_supported_transaction_version=0; reads fail as soon as the result contains a version 1 transaction.
maxSupportedTransactionVersion is set from a non-literal value; verify it resolves to 1 or higher.
Documentation or an AI skill shows maxSupportedTransactionVersion 0; readers and coding assistants copy it.
@solana/web3.js older than 1.99.0 cannot read a version 1 transaction at all: even with maxSupportedTransactionVersion 1 it rejects the response while parsing it.
Upgrading @solana/kit to 8.0.0 removes three compute-unit-limit helpers; code that calls them stops compiling.

probe.expect: Result has version 1 and no JSON-RPC error.

detect.summary: The project's transaction reader is run against a known version 1 transaction.

fix.summary: Pass maxSupportedTransactionVersion 1 in getTransaction and getBlock; with @solana/web3.js this also needs version 1.99.0 or later.
When moving to @solana/kit 8.0.0 or later, replace the compute-unit-limit helpers with the resource-limit helpers named in the release notes.

Set the maximum supported transaction version to 1 in the configuration of the RPC client (Some(1) in Rust, rpc.MaxSupportedTransactionVersion1 or uint64(1) in Go, max_supported_transaction_version=1 in Python), and check that the client library in use can decode a version 1 transaction.
